sections.title: Chapter 1
sections.subtitle: Prologue: On Holy Obedience, Humility, and the Vision of the Interior Castle

content.text: 1. Few tasks which I have been commanded to undertake by obedience have been so difficult to me as the present one of writing about prayer. For one reason, it seems to me that our Lord does not give me either the spirit or the desire for it; for another, my head has been in a continual state of noise and weakness for these past three months, so that it is painful for me even to write on necessary business.

2. But knowing that the strength given by obedience can make easy what seems impossible, my will submits with joy, although my weak nature seems greatly distressed. For our Lord has not given me so much virtue that my physical infirmities and constant occupations should not cause a great conflict in me. May He be pleased to guide this work, Who has helped me in many other more difficult undertakings, for in His divine mercy I place all my trust.

3. While I was beseeching our Lord today to speak through me, because I could find nothing to say nor did I know how to begin to obey this command, there came to my mind what I will now set down as a foundation for all that follows.

4. It is that we consider our soul to be like a castle made entirely out of a single diamond or very clear crystal, in which there are many rooms, just as in Heaven there are many mansions. (John 14:2) For if we reflect rightly, sisters, the soul of the just man is nothing else than a paradise wherein the Lord says He finds His delight. (Proverbs 8:31)

5. What, then, must that dwelling place be like wherein a King so powerful, so wise, so pure, and so full of all good things takes His delight? I can find nothing wherewith to compare the magnificent beauty and capacity of a soul; for truly our intellects, however sharp, can no more grasp it than they can comprehend God Himself, since He says that He created us in His own image and likeness. (Genesis 1:26)

6. It is no small shame and confusion that through our own fault we do not understand ourselves nor know who we are. Would it not be a great ignorance, my daughters, if someone were asked who he was, and did not know who his father or mother was or what country he belonged to? If that would be great stupidity, incomparably greater is the folly of not seeking to know what we are, but confining ourselves only to our bodies, knowing that we have a soul only because we have heard so by faith.

7. Let us now imagine that this castle contains many mansions, some above, others below, others at the sides, and in the center and midst of them all is the principal mansion, where the most secret things between God and the soul are transacted.

8. You must keep this comparison carefully in mind, for perhaps God will be pleased that by means of it I may be able to explain something of the graces He is pleased to bestow upon souls, and the differences between them, as far as I have understood it to be possible. No one can know them all, for they are manifold, and how much less one so wretched as I! For it will be a great comfort to you when the Lord grants them to know that it is possible, and to those who do not receive them, it will serve as a cause to praise His great goodness.

9. Let us return to our beautiful and delightful castle, and see how we can enter it. It seems that I am speaking nonsense, for if this castle is the soul, there is no need to enter it, since it is oneself; it would seem foolish to tell someone to enter a room when he is already in it. But you must understand that there are many ways of being in a place.

10. Many souls remain in the outer courtyard where the guards stand, and do not care to enter within, nor do they know what is in that most lovely place, nor who dwells there, nor what rooms there are. For as far as I have understood, the gate of entry into this castle is prayer and meditation. I do not say mental prayer more than vocal, for where there is prayer, it must be accompanied by reflection; and that prayer which is not accompanied by consideration of Whom one is addressing, and who it is that is speaking, and what is asked, I do not call prayer at all, however much the lips may move.

sections.title: Chapter 2
sections.subtitle: The First Mansions — Chapter 1: The Beauty and Dignity of the Soul in Grace and the Interior Castle

content.text: 1. Before speaking further, I wish you to consider what happens when the Sun of Justice, Who dwells in the center of the soul, diffuses His radiant light throughout all the mansions. How bright and beautiful that soul becomes, sharing in the divine splendor!

2. For as a fountain of pure water springing from a crystal source reflects the brightness of the sun in all its streams, so does the soul in the state of grace reflect the presence and beauty of God in all its works. Everything done in that soul is meritorious and pleasing in the sight of the Most High, because it springs from the true Source of all life. (Psalm 36:9; John 4:14)

3. But to enter the first mansions, the soul must make use of prayer, though it is still very absorbed in the world and plunged into its affairs, business, and pleasures. Such souls are surrounded by venomous creatures—reptiles, toads, and vipers—which dwell in the outskirts of the castle, that is, the senses and worldly attachments.

4. Yet it is a great mercy of God that they have even entered the outer rooms of the castle, for although they are in great danger, they are at least inside the walls. They do not yet perceive the great light that shines in the innermost chamber of the King, but they are closer to it than those outside who never pray at all.

5. Let those who are in this state take care not to turn back, but strive constantly to advance. They must realize that self-knowledge is the bread upon which all souls must feed, no matter how elevated their prayer may be. Without self-knowledge, the soul cannot make progress, for humility is the foundation of the whole interior castle.

6. In these first mansions, the light from the King's throne reaches only faintly, like light passing through thick clouds or frosted crystal. The soul must practice great vigilance, for the devil has countless snares prepared for those who are beginning to give themselves to prayer.

7. He knows well that if a soul perseveres in prayer, it is lost to him, and therefore he uses all his cunning to make it abandon its holy purpose. Let us fix our eyes on Christ, our true Good, and in Him we shall learn true humility and self-knowledge.

sections.title: Chapter 3
sections.subtitle: The First Mansions — Chapter 2: The Deformity of a Soul in Mortal Sin and the Necessity of Humility

content.text: 1. To understand the beauty of a soul in grace, it is very profitable to consider the misery and deformity of a soul in mortal sin. No darkness is so dense, no pitch so black and foul, that can be compared with the state of a soul that has turned away from God.

2. The Sun of Justice, although He remains in the center of the soul giving it being, is now hidden as behind a thick black veil. The soul is like a tree planted by the devil, which brings forth only poisonous and corrupt fruits. None of the good works done in that state can avail it for eternal life, because they do not proceed from the living principle of divine charity. (1 Corinthians 13:1-3)

3. O souls redeemed by the Blood of Jesus Christ, understand yourselves and take pity on your own misery! How is it possible that when you know this, you do not strive to remove the pitch and filth that obscures the crystal of your soul?

4. Remember that when the soul is in mortal sin, all the venomous beasts of the outer courtyard enter freely into the rooms, and the poor soul is in perpetual bondage and misery. It cannot enjoy the peace or light of the King Who created it for Himself.

5. Let us therefore ground ourselves firmly in humility. Humility is the truth: it shows us what we are of ourselves—nothingness, weakness, and sin—and what God is—infinite majesty, power, wisdom, and love. (Psalm 8:4-5)

6. The more a soul humbles itself, the more God exalts it, and the more safely it traverses the perilous mansions of this interior castle. Never let us imagine that we can make progress through our own strength or industry, but let us rely solely on the grace and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ.

sections.title: Chapter 4
sections.subtitle: The Second Mansions — Chapter 1: Warfare and Perseverance in Prayer Amidst Distractions

content.text: 1. In the Second Mansions are found those souls who have begun to practice prayer with greater determination and have understood the necessity of withdrawing from worldly occasions of sin, yet they still retain many attachments and suffer great warfare.

2. These souls understand the voice of God better than those in the first mansions, for the Lord calls them in many ways: through sermons, holy conversations, good books, sicknesses, and interior inspirations. (Hebrews 3:7-8)

3. But here the combat is far more severe, because the devil sees that the soul is slipping from his grasp. He sets before the imagination the pleasures, honors, and riches of the world, and tells the soul how hard is the path of virtue and mortification.

4. The soul hears the King calling it from within, while the world and the flesh call it from without. It is in the midst of this battle that perseverance is most urgently needed. Let the soul not abandon prayer, even if it feels dry, distracted, and beset by countless temptations.

5. It must cling to Christ crucified, knowing that He fought the battle before us and gained the victory for us. (Hebrews 12:2-3) Let it seek the companionship of good and spiritual persons, and avoid as pestilence the company of those who are tepid and worldly.

6. If the soul falls through human weakness, let it not give way to discouragement, which is a subtle form of pride, but let it rise promptly through sincere contrition and Confession, and return to the path of prayer with renewed confidence in God.

7. For our Lord does not look so much at the greatness of our works as at the love with which we do them. He desires our resolute determination to belong to Him alone, and He will never fail to give us His grace to conquer all obstacles.

sections.title: Chapter 5
sections.subtitle: The Third Mansions — Chapter 1: Orderly Devout Living, Penance, and the Danger of Spiritual Security

content.text: 1. By the great mercy of God, some souls overcome these combats and enter the Third Mansions. These are souls who live in the fear of the Lord, avoid mortal sin, practice vocal and mental prayer, keep their passions in order, distribute alms, and spend their time in useful and virtuous exercises.

2. Truly, this is a very desirable state, and there seems to be no reason why these souls should not be admitted to the innermost mansion of the King. Yet they are often in great danger of spiritual stagnation and false security, because they rely too much on their own well-regulated life.
3. They are like the rich young man in the Gospel who had kept all the commandments from his youth, yet when the Lord asked him to sell all and follow Him, he went away sorrowful. (Matthew 19:16-22)

4. They desire to serve God, but without losing their own comfort, reputation, or convenience. If any slight insult, contradiction, or illness comes upon them, they are easily upset and lose their peace of mind.

5. This shows that self-will and self-love are still very alive within them, although hidden under the appearance of virtue. They are very eager to impose penances upon themselves, but they bear with great impatience the penances which God sends them through others.

6. Let souls in this mansion understand that perfection does not consist in consolations or in doing many exterior works, but in conformity of our will to the will of God. They must ask for the virtue of holy obedience, and be willing to be treated as nothing for the love of Christ.

sections.title: Chapter 6
sections.subtitle: The Third Mansions — Chapter 2: Spiritual Dryness, Obedience, and Abandonment to the Divine Will

content.text: 1. It often happens that souls in the Third Mansions suffer great aridity and dryness in prayer, finding no sensible devotion or sweetness in their meditations.

2. They immediately think that all is lost and that God has abandoned them, or that they have committed some great fault. But this is a mistake: our Lord tests their fidelity and purifies their love, to see if they seek the God of consolations or the consolations of God.

3. We must learn to serve God at our own cost, without demanding wages of sensible delight. When aridity comes, let the soul humble itself, acknowledge its unworthiness, and resign itself completely into the hands of the Divine Potter. (Jeremiah 18:6; Isaiah 64:8)
4. True devotion consists in promptitude of will to do what God wills and what pleases Him most. If it pleases Him that we should remain in darkness and dryness, blessed be His holy Name! (Job 1:21)

5. The best remedy for the difficulties of this mansion is holy obedience to a wise spiritual director, abandoning our own judgment and letting ourselves be guided as little children. For the kingdom of heaven belongs to those who become like little children in simplicity and humility. (Matthew 18:3)

sections.title: Chapter 7
sections.subtitle: The Fourth Mansions — Chapter 1: Transition to Contemplation, Sweet Feelings vs Divine Delights

content.text: 1. Now we begin to treat of supernatural things, which cannot be attained by our own efforts or industry, however diligently we may labor, though we may dispose ourselves for them.
2. Here we must explain the difference between spiritual consolations, which I call contentos (sweet feelings), and divine delights, which I call gustos (spiritual savors).

3. Sweet feelings often arise from our own nature, helped by divine grace: when we meditate on the Passion, or weep over our sins, or rejoice in the glory of God. These feelings begin in our own understanding and will, and produce an emotion that affects even our bodily senses.

4. But divine delights (gustos) begin in God Himself and terminate in our nature; they arise from the innermost center of the soul and expand into the faculties with a sweetness and peace that words cannot describe. (Philippians 4:7)

5. In these Fourth Mansions, the intellect and imagination may still wander, but the soul must not be distressed by this. The mind is not the soul: the imagination is like a restless mill-clapper, but the will can remain quietly united to God in peace.
6. Let the soul not try to force the intellect to be still, but let it rest peacefully in the presence of the Lord, making acts of love and adoration without multiplying words or reasoning.

sections.title: Chapter 8
sections.subtitle: The Fourth Mansions — Chapter 2: The Prayer of Quiet and the Allegory of the Two Fountains

content.text: 1. To make you understand what I have said about the difference between contentos and gustos, I will use a comparison of two fountains of water that fill two large basins.

2. The first basin is filled with water brought from a great distance through many aqueducts and conduits by human skill and labor. This represents the consolations gained through our own meditations and ascetical efforts, where the water enters with noise and effort.

3. The second basin is built directly over the natural spring itself, so that the water rises from the very depths of the earth without any sound or pipe, filling the basin silently, abundantly, and overflowing in streams of living water. (John 7:38)

4. This represents the Prayer of Quiet, which is a true divine delight (gusto). It rises from the center of the soul, where God dwells, and produces an immense dilation and expansion of the heart, filling the entire interior with unspeakable peace and sweetness.

5. In this state, the will is captive and held in sweet surrender to God, while the other faculties—the memory and intellect—may still be free to move, but they cannot disturb the deep tranquility of the will.
6. The fruits of this prayer are great: a deep reverence for the Majesty of God, contempt for earthly vanity, a desire to suffer for Christ, and an increase in all solid virtues.

sections.title: Chapter 9
sections.subtitle: The Fourth Mansions — Chapter 3: The Prayer of Active Recollection and the Call of the Divine Shepherd

content.text: 1. There is another kind of prayer in these Fourth Mansions which is called Supernatural Recollection. It is not something we can acquire by thinking of God within ourselves, though that is a holy exercise which prepares the way.

2. It happens when the Divine Shepherd, Who dwells in the castle of the soul, sees the senses and faculties straying abroad among earthly things. In His infinite mercy, He gives a gentle interior call, like a soft whistle, which is heard in the secret depths of the soul. (Song of Songs 2:10)
3. At this voice, the senses and faculties retire from external objects and withdraw into the interior of the castle, just as bees enter the hive to make honey.

4. The soul realizes that it is in the presence of its Lord and feels drawn inward with great sweetness. When this happens, we must not strive to think of many things, nor force the intellect to be silent, for trying not to think only causes more thoughts.

5. Rather, let the soul surrender itself gently into the hands of God, enjoying His presence in love and humility, and saying with the young Samuel: "Speak, Lord, for Thy servant heareth." (1 Samuel 3:10)

sections.title: Chapter 10
sections.subtitle: The Fifth Mansions — Chapter 1: The Prayer of Union and Suspension of the Faculties

content.text: 1. O sisters! How shall I tell you of the riches, treasures, and delights which are found in the Fifth Mansions? It is better to say nothing of them, for neither can the intellect conceive them nor words express them.

2. In these mansions takes place the Prayer of Union. Here the soul is entirely asleep to the things of the world and to itself. During the short time that this union lasts, all the faculties—memory, intellect, and will—are completely suspended and absorbed in God.

3. The soul neither sees, nor hears, nor understands anything of the exterior world; it is so deeply joined to God that when it returns to itself, it cannot doubt that it was in God and God was in it. (John 14:20; 1 John 4:13)
4. This certainty is so absolute that even if many years should pass without the grace being repeated, the soul never forgets or doubts that it possessed God and was possessed by Him.
5. The duration of this prayer is very short; it rarely lasts for as long as half an hour, but while it lasts, the soul is transformed and enriched with immense spiritual treasures.
6. It comes out from this prayer with an ardent desire to praise God, a profound sorrow for past sins, and a total detachment from all created things.

sections.title: Chapter 11
sections.subtitle: The Fifth Mansions — Chapter 2: The Allegory of the Silkworm and the Butterfly of Divine Charity

content.text: 1. You will have heard of the wonderful way in which silk is made, an invention which only God could have devised. There are little seeds, like small peppercorns, which in the springtime, when the mulberry leaves begin to sprout, come to life and feed upon the leaves until they become large worms.

2. When they are full-grown, they begin with their little mouths to spin silk from their own substance, making a small cocoon in which they shut themselves up and die. And from that same cocoon, after a short time, there comes forth a white and lovely butterfly!

3. Who could have believed this if we had not seen it with our own eyes? This, sisters, is a wonderful emblem of the soul. The silkworm is the soul which begins to live by the heat of the Holy Spirit, feeding upon the nourishment provided by the Church in sermons, sacraments, and holy reading.

4. When it is full-grown in virtue and prayer, it begins to spin the cocoon of self-renunciation, dying to its own will, comforts, and desires. And when it is truly dead to itself in this Prayer of Union, it comes forth as a white butterfly of divine love! (Colossians 3:3; Galatians 2:20)

5. Now the soul is no longer crawling upon the earth, bound by earthly ties; it has wings to fly and cannot rest in anything of this world. It seeks only the honor of God and the salvation of souls, burning with the fire of supernatural charity.

sections.title: Chapter 12
sections.subtitle: The Fifth Mansions — Chapter 3: Another Degree of Union and Fraternal Charity as Proof of Love for God

content.text: 1. Do not imagine, daughters, that the only way to attain this union is through supernatural raptures and visions. There is another union which is far more secure and lasting, and which all of us can and should attain: the union of our will with the will of God.

2. The surest sign that we possess this true union is the love of our neighbor. For we cannot know with certainty whether we love God, although there are strong indications of it; but we can know very well whether we love our neighbor. (1 John 4:20-21)

3. The more you see yourself advancing in fraternal charity, the more certain you may be that you are advancing in the love of God. If we see a sister in need or sorrow, let us fly to her assistance, preferring her comfort to our own, even at great cost to ourselves.

4. If you practice this charity faithfully, our Lord will unite your will to His in such a manner that you will desire only what He desires. This is the union which I have desired all my life, and which I constantly ask of our Lord, for it is free from all danger of illusion.
5. Let us not build towers without foundations: the Lord does not look at the greatness of our works, but at the love with which they are performed.

sections.title: Chapter 13
sections.subtitle: The Fifth Mansions — Chapter 4: Vigilance in Union and Guarding Against Subtle Illusions

content.text: 1. Even when a soul has attained to these Fifth Mansions, it is not yet safe from falling back. The little butterfly must not be careless, for the devil has many snares prepared for it.

2. He sees that he cannot harm it directly by gross temptations to open sin, so he transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14), suggesting subtle imperfections under the appearance of good.

3. He makes the soul think it has attained great perfection, prompting it to judge others, to desire to teach before it has learned, or to undertake excessive penances that ruin health and prevent the performance of duty.
4. Let the soul walk in holy fear and perpetual vigilance, never trusting in its own past graces or spiritual experiences. (1 Corinthians 10:12)

5. The only safeguard is continuous humility, obedience, and self-distrust. Let us continually beg our Lord to uphold us with His hand, for if He leaves us for a single moment, we shall fall headlong into the abyss. (Psalm 73:23-24)

sections.title: Chapter 14
sections.subtitle: The Sixth Mansions — Chapter 1: The Spiritual Betrothal and Purifying External and Internal Trials

content.text: 1. Now we come to speak of the Sixth Mansions, where the soul is wounded with love for its Spouse and prepares for the Spiritual Marriage. But before this marriage can be consummated, the soul must pass through great and manifold purifications.

2. The first trial is the outcry of the world: praises that cause confusion and fear, and slanders, calumnies, and false judgments that are heaped upon the soul by good and bad alike. (Matthew 5:11-12)
3. The second trial is bodily sickness and severe physical infirmities, which our Lord often sends to purify the soul as gold in the furnace. (Wisdom 3:6)

4. The third and most terrible trial is an interior anguish and darkness of spirit, wherein the soul feels so unworthy and abandoned that it seems to have lost all faith, hope, and love. It feels that God has rejected it and that its past graces were delusions.

5. In this state, neither spiritual directors nor books can give any comfort, for God has closed the door to all consolation. The soul can only endure, resigning itself to suffer this martyrdom for as long as it shall please the divine Majesty.
6. Yet these trials are of priceless value: they cleanse the soul from all remaining rust of self-love and prepare it for the sublime favors of the King.

sections.title: Chapter 15
sections.subtitle: The Sixth Mansions — Chapter 2: The Wound of Love and Darts of Spiritual Yearning

content.text: 1. In these Sixth Mansions, our Lord often wounds the soul with a dart or arrow of fiery love, which penetrates to the very center of its being. (Song of Songs 2:5; Psalm 42:1-2)
2. It is not a physical wound, though it causes a sensible pain that makes the soul cry out, yet this pain is so delicious and sweet that the soul would never wish to be free from it.
3. The soul feels that its Beloved is present, yet He is hidden; it longs to enjoy Him fully and finds that the cage of the body is a prison that keeps it from its true Life. (Philippians 1:23)
4. This yearning consumes the soul with a thirst so intense that all created streams cannot quench it; only the living water of the fountain of God can satisfy its desire.
5. Blessed is that wound which brings such health, and blessed is that fire which purifies without destroying, kindling the heart with the eternal flames of the love of God!

sections.title: Chapter 16
sections.subtitle: The Sixth Mansions — Chapter 3: Divine Locutions and Discerning Authentic Words of God

content.text: 1. In this mansion, God is pleased to speak to the soul by means of divine locutions or interior words. These words are spoken in the secret of the heart, without sound of voice, yet with absolute clarity and power.
2. To distinguish true locutions from illusions or products of the imagination, three signs may be noted:

3. First, their supreme power and authority: when God speaks, the words work what they signify. If He says "Peace be with you," the soul is instantly filled with perfect peace, even in the midst of great tempest. (Mark 4:39)
4. Second, a great quietness and tranquility fills the soul, accompanied by profound humility and reverence.
5. Third, these words remain so engraved upon the memory that they are never forgotten, whereas words created by the mind soon vanish.

6. Let the soul never seek or desire to hear these locutions, for that would open the door to deception, but let it submit all things to its confessor and spiritual director with childlike simplicity.

sections.title: Chapter 17
sections.subtitle: The Sixth Mansions — Chapter 4: Raptures and Ecstasies and the Suspension of Bodily Senses

content.text: 1. Raptures and ecstasies are favors granted by God in which the soul is suddenly ravished and elevated above itself with an irresistible force.

2. The body loses its natural warmth and movement; the eyes cannot see, the ears cannot hear, and breathing seems almost suspended. The soul is so completely drawn into God that it feels as if it were leaving the body. (2 Corinthians 12:2-4)
3. In these raptures, God reveals to the soul secrets of His heavenly kingdom, celestial splendors, and mysteries of faith that no human language can describe.
4. When the soul returns to its normal state, it finds itself filled with immense courage, a boundless desire to suffer for Christ, and a total detachment from all earthly greatness.
5. The fear of death is entirely removed, for the soul has tasted something of the true life of heaven and longs to be dissolved and to be with Christ.

sections.title: Chapter 18
sections.subtitle: The Sixth Mansions — Chapter 5: The Flight of the Spirit and Mystical Elevation

content.text: 1. There is another kind of rapture which I call the Flight of the Spirit (el vuelo del espíritu). In this, the soul feels itself carried away with a swiftness so astonishing that it seems as if the spirit were separated from the body.

2. It is like a swift bird soaring into the highest heavens, leaving all earthly things far beneath it. From that sublime height, the soul looks down upon the world and sees how petty, transient, and worthless are all its honors, riches, and pleasures.
3. It perceives that this present life is but a shadow and a dream, and it grieves for those who spend their days pursuing smoke and vanity. (Ecclesiastes 1:2)
4. This grace leaves behind it a profound humility, for the soul sees that it was lifted up entirely by the mercy of God without any merit of its own, and that of itself it is only dust and ashes.

sections.title: Chapter 19
sections.subtitle: The Sixth Mansions — Chapter 6: The Agony of Love and Sorrow in Separation from God

content.text: 1. Among the favors of this mansion, there is one which causes the soul an agony so intense that it seems as if life must end. It is a spiritual sorrow born of the intense longing to be united with God, while realizing that it is still exiled in this valley of tears. (Psalm 120:5)

2. The soul sees the infinite beauty, goodness, and majesty of its Beloved, and the impossibility of enjoying Him fully in this mortal body. It is suspended between heaven and earth: earth can give it no comfort, and heaven is not yet attained.
3. This pain is far greater than any bodily torment, yet it is so cherished by the soul that it would not exchange it for all the kingdoms of the world.
4. In this crucible of love, the soul is thoroughly refined, all its earthly affections are burnt away, and it is prepared to receive the crown of perfect union.

sections.title: Chapter 20
sections.subtitle: The Sixth Mansions — Chapter 7: The Sacred Humanity of Jesus Christ as Universal Foundation

content.text: 1. I wish to warn you against a great error into which some persons fall: they think that when they have attained to contemplation, they should set aside the Sacred Humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ and meditate only on the pure Divinity.
2. This is a very dangerous mistake! Christ is the Way, the Truth, and the Life: no one comes to the Father except through Him. (John 14:6) He is the Door through which all must enter. (John 10:9)
3. If we turn away from our only Guide, how can we hope to reach the goal safely? In the Sacred Humanity of Jesus we find our model, our strength, and our refuge in all trials and temptations.

4. St. Paul says that he determined to know nothing among the Corinthians except Jesus Christ and Him crucified. (1 Corinthians 2:2) Let us walk with Him, suffer with Him, and contemplate His holy life and Passion at every stage of the spiritual life.

5. When God is pleased to suspend our faculties in higher contemplation, we must receive His gift with thanksgiving, but when we are left to our own activity, we must never deliberately abandon the contemplation of our Lord's Sacred Humanity.

sections.title: Chapter 21
sections.subtitle: The Sixth Mansions — Chapter 8: Intellectual Visions and the Direct Perception of Christ

content.text: 1. God is also pleased to grant intellectual visions, in which the soul perceives the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ or of the saints, without seeing any form, shape, or color either with the bodily eyes or with the imagination.
2. It is a direct and certain spiritual awareness, clearer than any sight of the eyes, whereby the soul knows with infallible certainty that Christ is standing at its right hand. (Psalm 16:8)
3. This presence brings with it great light, strength, and continuous recollection. The soul feels accompanied at all times by its divine Master, and is filled with reverent fear and holy love.
4. This vision does not come and go quickly like imaginary visions, but may last for many days, weeks, or even months, producing marvelous fruits of holiness and conformity to Christ.

sections.title: Chapter 22
sections.subtitle: The Sixth Mansions — Chapter 9: Imaginary Visions and Divine Visual Manifestations

content.text: 1. Imaginary visions are those wherein our Lord manifests Himself to the interior sense of the soul in some sacred form, such as in His Resurrection, His Passion, or in His glorious majesty.
2. These visions do not enter through the bodily eyes, but are represented to the imagination with a beauty and splendor that far exceeds all earthly comparisons.
3. The glory of the risen Christ is so radiant that a single glimpse of His countenance is enough to ravish the soul for a lifetime, filling it with boundless joy and courage.

4. The devil can counterfeit imaginary visions, but the true visions of God may be known by the fruits they produce: deep humility, contempt of self, increase of charity, and submission to the Church and one's spiritual director.

sections.title: Chapter 23
sections.subtitle: The Sixth Mansions — Chapter 10: Intellectual Visions of High Theological Truths and the Divine Mirror

content.text: 1. In these higher chambers of the Sixth Mansions, God communicates to the soul intellectual visions of sublime theological mysteries, such as the unity and trinity of God, and how all creatures are present in Him.

2. The soul sees in God, as in a clear and boundless mirror, all created things reflected without any confusion. It understands how God sees all our thoughts, actions, and desires at every moment. (Hebrews 4:13)
3. This knowledge produces in the soul a holy fear of offending a God Who is so present and so pure, and an immense appreciation of the beauty and wisdom displayed in creation.
4. The soul also perceives something of the infinite purity and holiness of God, in comparison with which our greatest righteousness is but filthy rags. (Isaiah 64:6)

sections.title: Chapter 24
sections.subtitle: The Sixth Mansions — Chapter 11: Final Purification and the Martyrdom of Burning Love

content.text: 1. Before entering the Seventh Mansions, the soul must undergo a final and vehement martyrdom of burning love.
2. The Lord enkindles in the soul a desire so intense and a love so impetuous that it feels as if it were being torn apart by the violence of its desire to be united with God.
3. It is like a soul suspended between life and death: it cannot live without God, yet it cannot possess Him fully while on earth.
4. In this final purification, the last remnants of self-seeking and attachment are consumed, leaving the soul pure, transparent, and completely disposed for the Spiritual Marriage.

sections.title: Chapter 25
sections.subtitle: The Seventh Mansions — Chapter 1: Entry into the Innermost Mansion and the Indwelling of the Trinity

content.text: 1. Now we come to speak of the Seventh Mansions, the innermost sanctuary of the castle, where the King of glory makes His permanent dwelling in the center of the soul.
2. When the soul is brought into this mansion, the Most Holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—reveals Itself to the intellect in an intellectual vision of astonishing clarity. (John 14:23)
3. The soul understands with great certitude that all Three Persons are in the center of its being, and that They never depart from it, although the sensible perception of Their presence may vary.
4. The soul enjoys a continuous and intimate conversation with its God, living in the company of the Holy Trinity in a peace that surpasses all human understanding. (Philippians 4:7)

5. This presence does not hinder the soul from attending to its exterior duties and business; rather, the spirit remains quietly anchored in God while the faculties perform their daily work in charity.

sections.title: Chapter 26
sections.subtitle: The Seventh Mansions — Chapter 2: The Transforming Union and the Indissoluble Spiritual Marriage

content.text: 1. In this Seventh Mansion takes place the Spiritual Marriage, which differs from the Spiritual Betrothal as an indissoluble bond differs from a promise of marriage.
2. In the Spiritual Betrothal, the union is temporary and the soul may still experience separations; but in the Spiritual Marriage, the union is permanent and transforming.

3. It is like two wax candles whose wicks are joined together in one flame, so that they can no longer be separated; or like rain falling into a river, where the water of the stream and the water of the rain become one and the same water. (1 Corinthians 6:17)
4. The soul is transformed in God by participation in His divine nature, so that it can say with the Apostle: "I live, now not I, but Christ liveth in me." (Galatians 2:20)
5. There are no longer any violent raptures or ecstasies, because the soul has been strengthened to bear the divine presence without physical weakness or disturbance.

sections.title: Chapter 27
sections.subtitle: The Seventh Mansions — Chapter 3: Sublime Peace and Fruitful Tranquility of the Seventh Mansion

content.text: 1. The fruits of this Seventh Mansion are peace, tranquility, and an extraordinary liberty of spirit.
2. The venomous reptiles and wild beasts of the outer courtyard can no longer enter this innermost chamber, for the King has placed a guard around it.
3. The soul experiences no more interior unrest or fear of damnation; its only desire is that God's will be done in all things, whether in life or in death, in suffering or in joy.
4. It has a great love for its persecutors and for all who do it harm, desiring their spiritual welfare with sincere affection. (Matthew 5:44)
5. It is eager to suffer all things for Christ, yet it does not seek suffering with anxiety, but rests peacefully in whatever God ordains.

sections.title: Chapter 28
sections.subtitle: The Seventh Mansions — Chapter 4: The True End of Mystical Union in Apostolic Service and Charity

content.text: 1. Do not think, sisters, that the purpose of all these sublime graces is merely to give spiritual delights and consolations to the soul.
2. The true end and purpose of the Spiritual Marriage is the birth of good works, the service of God, and the salvation of our neighbor! (John 15:16)
3. Martha and Mary must join together to welcome the Lord and offer Him hospitality: Mary sits at His feet in contemplative prayer, while Martha serves Him in active charity. (Luke 10:38-42)
4. If Mary had remained idle without Martha's service, who would have provided food for our Lord and His disciples? Contemplation and action must go hand in hand.

5. Let all our prayer, desires, and mortifications be directed toward the glory of God and the benefit of Holy Church. For this you were called, daughters, and this is the true crown of the interior castle!

sections.title: Chapter 29
sections.subtitle: Epilogue: Concluding Reflections, Submission to Holy Mother Church, and Blessing

content.text: 1. Although this castle contains many more mansions than I have described, these few will suffice for you, my sisters.
2. You do not need to ask permission from your superiors to enter these mansions, for you may enter whenever you will through humble and persevering prayer.
3. In all that I have written, I submit myself entirely to the judgment and correction of our Holy Mother the Roman Catholic Church, ready to retract whatever may be found contrary to the true faith.
4. If there is anything good in this book, it belongs entirely to God, Who has chosen so poor an instrument to manifest His glory; whatever is defective is mine alone.

5. May our Lord Jesus Christ be praised and blessed forever and ever, and may He grant us all the grace to reach that innermost mansion where He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, world without end. Amen.
